narrative:
The 2024 Pittsburgh Pirates were a team of fleeting promise and accumulated disappointment, a club that spent the better part of six months proving it was close enough to be interesting but not quite good enough to matter. They opened the year with an encouraging 4-0 spring, and early regular-season fireworks — Rowdy Tellez launching a three-run shot on Opening Day — gave the city reasons to believe. But the bullpen, and specifically closer David Bednar, would become a recurring source of heartbreak. As early as Opening Night, Bednar surrendered a walk-off homer that erased the joy Tellez had created, setting a pattern that would haunt Pittsburgh all year long.

April crumbled to a 10-17 mark despite individual flashes: Bryan Reynolds knocking clutch home runs, Oneil Cruz slashing rockets into the gaps. May and June offered some balance, the Pirates hovering near .500 and occasionally looking like contenders — Cruz's towering doubles in May, a Yasmani Grandal three-run blast, the team winning a series here and there. July brought the best sustained stretch of baseball the Pirates played all year, a 15-10 month that briefly stirred postseason arithmetic, powered by a Nick Gonzales walk-off single and Michael A. Taylor's three-run home run giving the club back-to-back thrills.

Then August arrived and swallowed everything whole. An 8-19 disaster month featured Bednar surrendering leads in the most crushing of circumstances — giving up a walk-off single on August 28th with a WPA swing of -0.627, among the most damaging moments of the season. Colin Holderman, Aroldis Chapman, and the bullpen in general became synonymous with late-game catastrophe. By the time September rolled around, the playoffs were a mathematical fantasy. Chapman's double allowed on September 7th — a -0.665 swing — put an exclamation point on a season of bullpen failures. The Pirates finished 76-86, outscored by 74 runs, relying on youth, hope, and the occasional Grandal home run to remind themselves what winning felt like.

For all its frustrations, the 2024 Pirates were not without their story lines. Grandal's pinch-hit blast on August 25th — a stunning +0.821 WPA swing, the single most impactful positive play of the season — captured the way Pittsburgh could electrify its fans without warning. Rookie Billy Cook hit his first career home run in September, a three-run shot that suggested the next chapter might be brighter. The rotation held its own with a respectable 4.15 ERA, and Cruz and Reynolds showed they could anchor an offense capable of something more. But 2024 ultimately belonged to the ledger of seasons that built toward something, rather than arriving at it.

chapters.title: Opening Sparks, Opening Wounds
chapters.description: The Pirates roar out of the gate with Tellez's Opening Day homer, then immediately suffer the bullpen agony that would define their year.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: Through April's rough patch and into May and June, individual heroics from Reynolds, Cruz, and Grandal keep Pittsburgh afloat near .500.

chapters.title: July Surge
chapters.description: The Pirates post their best month at 15-10, with clutch hits from Nick Gonzales and Michael A. Taylor briefly igniting playoff dreams.

chapters.title: August Collapse
chapters.description: An 8-19 August destroys any postseason hopes, as the bullpen — especially Bednar — implodes in one devastating late-inning loss after another.

chapters.title: Playing Out the String
chapters.description: September offers little salvation but flashes of the future, including Billy Cook's first career home run, as the Pirates close out a losing season with their eyes on what's next.
